subChunks.title: Hypothesis Formation
subChunks.hookHtml: A hypothesis is not a hunch, a hope, or a vague suspicion. It is a knife-edged claim that the world can refuse — and the sharpness of that edge is what separates science from wishful thinking.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The shape of a falsifiable hypothesis

Karl Popper, in Logik der Forschung (1934), argued that the defining feature of a scientific claim is not that it can be proven true, but that it can be proven false. A hypothesis must, in principle, be capable of being contradicted by some observable evidence. If no possible observation could refute the claim, the claim is not scientific — whatever else it may be.

A well-formed hypothesis usually takes a form like:

Increasing X by [measurable amount]
causes Y to change by [measurable amount]
under [specified conditions].

Notice the three parts: a cause, an effect, and the conditions under which the relationship holds. "Sleep deprivation impairs short-term memory" is the seed of a hypothesis. "Reducing nightly sleep from 8 hours to 4 hours for 7 consecutive days reduces digit-span recall by at least 15% in healthy adults aged 20–35" is a hypothesis you can test.

Null vs alternative

Every empirical study has two competing claims running silently in the background:

  • The null hypothesis (H0) — there is no effect, the groups are the same, the intervention does nothing
  • The alternative hypothesis (H1) — there is an effect, in a specified direction or magnitude

Statistical tests do not directly confirm H1. They ask: if H0 were true, how surprising would this data be? If the answer is "very surprising," we tentatively reject H0 in favour of H1. We never "prove" H1; we only fail to reject it. This asymmetry is built into the method on purpose, and we will return to it in sci-a3.

Why "X might affect Y" is not a hypothesis

A scientific hypothesis must commit. "Caffeine might affect alertness" forbids nothing — caffeine increasing alertness, decreasing it, or doing nothing all leave the claim intact. A hypothesis that cannot lose is not science. Compare:

  • Not a hypothesis: "Stress is related to heart disease." (In what direction? At what magnitude? Under what conditions?)
  • A hypothesis: "Sustained workplace stress (≥40 hrs/week of self-reported high stress for ≥6 months) raises resting systolic blood pressure by ≥5 mmHg in adults with no prior cardiovascular diagnosis."

Operationalisation

To turn an idea into a hypothesis, every fuzzy concept must be operationalised — defined in terms of something measurable. "Intelligence," "happiness," "productivity," "stress" all need an explicit operational definition before testing. "Stress" might be operationalised as a score on the Perceived Stress Scale (Cohen, Kamarck & Mermelstein 1983), or as salivary cortisol levels at 8am, or as self-reported hours per week. These three operationalisations would give you three different studies. The claim that emerges is bound to the operational definition you chose — and a different definition could yield a contradictory result.

Hypotheses don't appear from nowhere

Good hypotheses come from prior knowledge — published literature, pilot data, theoretical models, observed anomalies. The naïve picture of science as "observe, then hypothesise" is misleading. A hypothesis is shaped by the body of work it sits in, and any honest hypothesis paper begins with a literature review explaining why this particular claim is worth testing now. A hypothesis untethered from prior work is usually either trivial (already established) or doomed (already refuted).
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
📜 Sharpen a vague claim

Take this vague claim: "Exercise improves mood." Rewrite it as a falsifiable hypothesis. You should specify:

  • What kind of exercise, for how long, at what frequency
  • How "mood" will be measured (named scale, salivary marker, behavioural outcome)
  • The population you're claiming the effect for
  • The minimum effect size you would consider meaningful

Then state the corresponding null hypothesis. Notice how much you had to commit to before the sentence became something the world could refuse.

storyBeats.text: You enter a low-ceilinged stone workshop. Glass retorts steam on a long bench; copper coils descend into bowls of dark fluid. A wiry figure in a stained leather apron does not look up — she is writing in a margin, in red ink, the word WRONG.

storyBeats.speaker: Master Vesper
storyBeats.text: Sit. Don't touch the green flask. (she finishes the note, sets the quill down) I have been wrong, apprentice, more times than I can count. Once I lost three months chasing a hypothesis that could not be refuted by any experiment I could devise. It was a belief, not a hypothesis, and I had not noticed the difference. You will start where I should have started — by learning what a hypothesis actually is.

storyBeats.speaker: Master Vesper
storyBeats.text: A hypothesis is a claim the world is permitted to refuse. "This tincture cures fevers" is not a hypothesis until you say which fevers, in whom, by how much, measured how, over what window. Every fuzzy word is a place the claim wriggles free of being wrong. Pin it down. If after pinning, no possible experiment could falsify it — throw it away. It is theology, not chemistry.

storyBeats.speaker: Vague claim → testable hypothesis
storyBeats.text:
Vague:    "Sleep helps memory."

Hypothesis:
  Reducing nightly sleep from 8 hours to 4 hours
  for 7 consecutive nights
  reduces digit-span recall scores by ≥15%
  in healthy adults aged 20–35.

Null (H0): The change in digit-span recall is
           not different from zero.
Alt  (H1): The change is a reduction of ≥15%.

storyBeats.speaker: Master Vesper
storyBeats.text: Note the asymmetry. Statistics never proves the alternative. It only tells you whether the data would be surprising under the null. Knowing the difference between "failed to reject the null" and "the alternative is true" will save you from writing a paper that has to be retracted. I have written one. I do not recommend the experience.

storyBeats.speaker: Master Vesper
storyBeats.text: And no — hypotheses do not fall from the sky. The good ones come from reading. From noticing the gap between what a published study claimed and what it actually showed. From a pilot that surprised you. From a theory that predicted X and you saw not-X. If your hypothesis cannot point to the prior work that made it a question worth asking, you are guessing in the dark.

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a curious friend why "meditation might affect anxiety" is not yet a scientific hypothesis. Show them the smallest set of words you'd add to make it one — then state the null hypothesis it implies.

questions.questionHtml: According to Popper (1934), what distinguishes a scientific claim from a non-scientific one?
options: It must be capable, in principle, of being refuted by some observation
It must have been confirmed by at least one experiment
It must be expressed in mathematical language
It must be approved by a recognised academic authority
questions.correctAnswer: It must be capable, in principle, of being refuted by some observation
questions.explanationHtml: Popper's demarcation criterion is falsifiability. A scientific claim must specify what would count as evidence against it. Claims that no observation could possibly refute ("there is an invisible undetectable force") may be true, but they are not scientific.

questions.questionHtml: Which of the following is the only one that qualifies as a falsifiable scientific hypothesis?
options: Drinking 400mg of caffeine within 30 minutes of a digit-span test increases mean recall by at least 8% in caffeine-naive adults
Caffeine has interesting effects on the human brain
Many people feel more alert after coffee
Caffeine might be either a stimulant or a depressant depending on the person
questions.correctAnswer: Drinking 400mg of caffeine within 30 minutes of a digit-span test increases mean recall by at least 8% in caffeine-naive adults
questions.explanationHtml: Only the first option specifies a cause (400mg caffeine), an effect (≥8% increase in digit-span recall), conditions (within 30 min, caffeine-naive adults), and is therefore something an experiment could refute. The others are too vague to be wrong — and a claim that cannot lose is not a hypothesis.

questions.questionHtml: What does "operationalising" a concept like "stress" mean?
options: Defining it in terms of something concrete and measurable (e.g. a named scale, a biomarker, a behaviour)
Translating it into a different language
Confirming it with a group of expert reviewers
Removing it from the hypothesis to simplify the study
questions.correctAnswer: Defining it in terms of something concrete and measurable (e.g. a named scale, a biomarker, a behaviour)
questions.explanationHtml: Operationalisation turns a fuzzy concept into something a study can actually measure — for example, defining "stress" as a score on the Perceived Stress Scale (Cohen et al. 1983) or as 8am salivary cortisol. The conclusion of the study is then bound to that specific operational definition.

questions.questionHtml: A friend says: "I think mindfulness practice could be helpful for some people who are anxious." Why is this not yet a scientific hypothesis, even though it sounds reasonable?
options: It commits to nothing measurable — "could be", "some people", "anxious" are all unspecified, so no possible observation would contradict it
Mindfulness has not yet been studied scientifically
It uses informal language instead of a formula
Friends are not allowed to formulate hypotheses
questions.correctAnswer: It commits to nothing measurable — "could be", "some people", "anxious" are all unspecified, so no possible observation would contradict it
questions.explanationHtml: Every fuzzy term is a place the claim escapes refutation. "Could be" admits any outcome. "Some people" is unfalsifiable (there's always someone). "Anxious" needs an operational definition. To make this a hypothesis you must commit: which population, what dose of mindfulness, measured how, expected to change by how much.

subChunks.title: Controlled Experiments & Variables
subChunks.hookHtml: An experiment that cannot rule out alternative explanations is not an experiment — it is an anecdote with a sample size. Control is what turns observation into evidence.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Independent and dependent variables

Every experiment has at least two variables. The independent variable (IV) is the one you change; the dependent variable (DV) is the one you measure to see whether your change had an effect. "Does caffeine improve reaction time?" — caffeine dose is the IV; reaction time is the DV.

Everything else that could plausibly influence the DV is a potential confounding variable. The whole craft of experimental design is the systematic elimination of confounds.

Confounding variables and how to control for them

Suppose you measure reaction time before and after coffee, and reaction time improves. The coffee did it — right? Maybe. Or:

  • The participants got better simply by practising the task (a practice effect)
  • The coffee shop was warmer than the morning room (temperature confound)
  • Time of day shifted alertness independently (circadian confound)
  • Participants knew they had drunk coffee and expected to be faster (expectancy effect)

Control means designing the study so each of these alternative explanations cannot, by construction, account for the result.

Random assignment vs random selection (different things)

These get confused constantly. They are not the same.

  • Random selection — how participants are recruited from a population. Affects the generalisability of the result. Without random selection, your finding may only apply to whoever you happened to sample.
  • Random assignment — how participants are allocated to treatment groups. Affects the internal validity of the causal claim. Without random assignment, group differences could be due to who ended up in which group rather than the treatment.

You can have random assignment without random selection (a treatment study on undergraduates who happened to volunteer) and random selection without random assignment (a national survey with no intervention). The two answer different questions.

Blinding and placebo controls

If participants know they are receiving the active treatment, expectancy alone can change the outcome — the placebo effect. If experimenters know who got what, they may unconsciously rate outcomes more favourably for the treatment group — the experimenter effect.

  • Single-blind — participants don't know their group; experimenters do
  • Double-blind — neither participants nor experimenters know group assignment until the data is analysed
  • Placebo — an inactive treatment indistinguishable from the active one, given to the control group

Within- vs between-subjects, and counterbalancing

A between-subjects design assigns different participants to different conditions. A within-subjects design has every participant experience every condition. Within-subjects controls for individual differences (each person is their own control) but introduces order effects — fatigue, learning, carry-over from one condition to the next. The fix is counterbalancing: half the participants get condition A then B, the other half get B then A. Order is now a balanced confound rather than a hidden one.

Why correlation doesn't establish causation

Two variables can correlate for at least four distinct reasons:

  1. X causes Y (the conclusion you want)
  2. Y causes X (reverse causation)
  3. A third variable Z causes both X and Y (confounding)
  4. Coincidence in a finite sample (chance)

To establish causation you need designs that rule out (2), (3), and (4). The gold standard is the randomised controlled trial (RCT) — random assignment to treatment vs control breaks the link between Z and treatment-status, leaving (1) as the most parsimonious explanation when an effect appears. Where RCTs are impossible (you cannot ethically assign people to smoke), causal inference uses natural experiments, instrumental variables, regression discontinuity, and similar quasi-experimental tools — each ruling out specific confounds in different ways.
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
📜 Find the confound

A study reports: "Students who attended the new optional study skills workshop scored 12% higher on final exams than students who did not attend." The author concludes the workshop caused the improvement.

  • Identify three plausible confounding variables
  • For each, explain how it could produce the observed correlation without the workshop having any causal effect
  • Describe an experimental design (random assignment to attend or not) that would rule them out

Once you've done this for the workshop, try the same exercise with: "Cities with more parks have lower obesity rates."

storyBeats.text: Master Vesper has set out two identical clay cups, each filled with a pale infusion. She has also produced a small mechanical timer.

storyBeats.speaker: Master Vesper
storyBeats.text: I once sold a tincture I was certain sharpened the wits. Every customer reported feeling more clear-headed. I was, as it turned out, an idiot — they were paying coin for it. Of course they reported improvement. (taps the cups) One of these is the tincture. The other is hot water with a drop of lemon. Neither of us knows which is which — my apprentice swapped them this morning and labelled them A and B. That is what we call double-blinding.

storyBeats.speaker: Master Vesper
storyBeats.text: Now. I claim the tincture sharpens reaction time. To test it I must hold everything constant except the tincture. The room temperature. The time of day. The task you do. Anything that varies with the tincture and could plausibly cause the effect — what we call a confound — has to be either fixed or randomised away.

storyBeats.speaker: Two designs for the same question
storyBeats.text:
BAD design (uncontrolled):
  Take tincture in the morning,
  do reaction-time task in the evening.
  Compare against yesterday's morning score.

  Confounds: time-of-day, practice effect,
  expectancy, what you ate for lunch...

BETTER design (RCT):
  100 volunteers, randomly assigned to
  treatment (tincture) or control (placebo).
  Both groups do the same task at the same time
  in the same room, neither group knows which
  cup they drank, neither does the rater.
  Compare group means.

storyBeats.speaker: Master Vesper
storyBeats.text: Two terms get muddled. Random selection is how you choose who takes part — it tells you whether the result generalises. Random assignment is how you decide which group each person ends up in — it tells you whether the result is causal. They are different. You can have one without the other. A study on a hundred volunteer apprentices can still be a clean RCT — it just won't generalise to royal courtiers.

storyBeats.speaker: Master Vesper
storyBeats.text: And remember — correlation is not causation. The number of pirates and the average global temperature have correlated for two centuries. Either one drives the other, or some third thing drives both, or it is coincidence. To untangle: assign at random and break the link. Where you cannot assign — smoking, schooling, war, weather — you reach for natural experiments, instrumental variables, regression discontinuity. Each is a different knife for a different confound.

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to someone who has never read a study why "people who eat breakfast weigh less" does not mean breakfast causes lower weight. Walk them through three rival explanations and how a randomised controlled trial would rule them out.

questions.questionHtml: What is the difference between random selection and random assignment?
options: Random selection is how participants are recruited from a population (affects generalisability); random assignment is how they are allocated to groups (affects internal validity)
They are different names for the same procedure
Random selection is for surveys; random assignment is for animal studies
Random selection is mandatory in science; random assignment is optional
questions.correctAnswer: Random selection is how participants are recruited from a population (affects generalisability); random assignment is how they are allocated to groups (affects internal validity)
questions.explanationHtml: The two procedures answer different questions. Random selection lets you generalise from sample to population. Random assignment lets you draw causal inferences from treatment to outcome. A study can have one without the other — and most volunteer-based RCTs have random assignment without random selection.

questions.questionHtml: A pharmaceutical study finds that patients given a new sleep drug fall asleep 22 minutes faster than the previous week. The researchers conclude the drug works. What is the most serious flaw in this design?
options: There is no control group, so any change could be due to placebo, time, regression to the mean, or other confounds rather than the drug
The sample is too small
Sleep is too subjective to measure
The dose was probably wrong
questions.correctAnswer: There is no control group, so any change could be due to placebo, time, regression to the mean, or other confounds rather than the drug
questions.explanationHtml: Without a control group receiving placebo, you cannot separate the drug's effect from the placebo effect, the natural course of the condition, regression to the mean (people often enrol when sleeping particularly badly, then drift back toward their average), or the simple passage of time. A randomised controlled trial with placebo is the standard fix.

questions.questionHtml: An education researcher gives every student a memory-training programme and a memory test before and after. Test scores improve. Which of these is the strongest threat to the conclusion that the programme caused the improvement?
options: Practice effect — students may have improved simply by taking the test twice, regardless of the programme
The students might have liked the programme
Memory is hard to define
The researcher should have used a longer test
questions.correctAnswer: Practice effect — students may have improved simply by taking the test twice, regardless of the programme
questions.explanationHtml: Pre/post designs without a control group are vulnerable to practice effects, maturation, history, and regression to the mean. The fix is a control group that takes the same pre-test and post-test but does NOT receive the programme. If the treatment group improves more than the control, the difference is attributable to the programme.

questions.questionHtml: A study finds a strong correlation between coffee consumption and risk of heart attack. A journalist concludes that coffee causes heart attacks. List the four classes of explanation a careful reader must consider before accepting causation.
options: Coffee causes heart attacks (X→Y); heart-attack risk causes coffee drinking (Y→X); a third variable like stress causes both (Z→X and Z→Y); chance in a finite sample
Only chance — correlation is meaningless without a p-value below 0.05
The data must have been collected wrongly
There is only one possibility, so causation can be assumed
questions.correctAnswer: Coffee causes heart attacks (X→Y); heart-attack risk causes coffee drinking (Y→X); a third variable like stress causes both (Z→X and Z→Y); chance in a finite sample
questions.explanationHtml: Any observed correlation has at minimum these four candidate explanations. (Reverse causation here is plausible: people at high cardiovascular risk may self-medicate with stimulants, or the relationship may reverse after adjusting for smoking.) Untangling them requires designs that can rule out the alternatives — RCTs where ethical, instrumental variables and regression discontinuity where not.

subChunks.title: Statistical Reasoning
subChunks.hookHtml: Most people misunderstand p-values. Most people misunderstand confidence intervals. Most people misunderstand statistical power. The result is decades of published findings that turn out, on replication, not to be there. Statistical literacy is not optional — it is the difference between knowledge and noise.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
What a p-value actually means

A p-value is the probability of observing data at least as extreme as the data you got, assuming the null hypothesis is true. That is all it is. In symbols:

p = P(data this extreme or more | H0 is true)

What it is not:

  • The probability that the null is true
  • The probability that the alternative is true
  • The probability the result was "due to chance"
  • An effect-size measure

A study of 50,000 people can produce p < 0.001 for an effect that is too small to matter to anyone. A study of 30 people can fail to reach p < 0.05 for an effect that is real and substantial. The p-value is sensitive to both effect size and sample size, and reading one without the other will mislead you every time.

Effect sizes — why p alone is uninformative

An effect size measures the magnitude of a difference, independent of sample size. Common ones:

  • Cohen's d — the difference between two means in standard-deviation units. Cohen (1988) suggested rules of thumb: d = 0.2 small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large. These are conventions, not laws.
  • r and r² — correlation and the proportion of variance explained. r² = 0.01 means the predictor explains 1% of the variance, even if p is tiny.
  • Odds ratios, risk ratios — for binary outcomes (sick / not sick).

Reporting standards (the APA's, since 1994; tightened in 2010) require effect size alongside p. A modern paper that reports only p-values is doing it wrong.

Confidence intervals

A 95% confidence interval is a range constructed so that, over many repetitions of the study, 95% of such intervals would contain the true population value. It is not the probability that the true value is in this particular interval (frequentist statistics does not let you say that). For practical purposes, a CI gives you the same information as a p-value plus an effect-size estimate plus a precision estimate, all in one. Many statisticians prefer them for this reason.

Power and the four-cell decision matrix

Every test of H0 can succeed or fail in two ways:

Reject H0Fail to reject H0
H0 is trueType I error (false positive, rate α, usually 0.05)Correct
H0 is falseCorrect (rate 1 − β, called power)Type II error (false negative, rate β)

Statistical power is the probability of correctly rejecting a false null — i.e. of detecting a real effect when one exists. Conventional target is 0.80. An underpowered study with a real effect will frequently miss it; worse, when an underpowered study does reach significance, the effect size is systematically inflated (Gelman & Carlin 2014). Always ask: what was the power calculation? A post-hoc "we ran what we could afford" is not a power calculation.

Multiple comparisons and the garden of forking paths

If you run 20 independent tests, each at α = 0.05, you expect about 1 significant result purely by chance, even if no real effects exist. This is the multiple comparisons problem. Bonferroni correction (divide α by the number of tests) is a blunt fix; false-discovery-rate procedures (Benjamini & Hochberg 1995) are more powerful but still require pre-specification.

The deeper version, identified by Gelman & Loken (2014), is the garden of forking paths: even an honest researcher running a single analysis is implicitly choosing between many possible analyses (which outliers to drop, which transformation to use, which covariates to control for). Each unreported choice inflates the effective false-positive rate. The defence is pre-registration — committing to the analysis plan in writing before seeing the data.

Bayesian reasoning, briefly

Frequentist statistics asks "how surprising is this data under H0?" Bayesian statistics asks the more useful question: "given my prior beliefs and this data, what should I now believe?"

posterior  ∝  prior  ×  likelihood

Bayesian inference forces you to state your prior — what you thought before seeing the data — and updates it. A surprising result against a strong prior should move belief less than a surprising result against a weak prior. Ioannidis (2005), in Why Most Published Research Findings Are False, used essentially this Bayesian intuition to argue that in fields with weak priors and many tests, the posterior probability that a published positive finding is true can be well below 50%. The argument is uncomfortable. It is also approximately right — the replication crisis (sci-a4) is what it predicted.
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
📜 Read a result honestly

A study reports: "Patients given the supplement scored higher on the cognition test (p = 0.04, n = 50 per group)."

  • What does the p-value of 0.04 mean? (State it precisely — and what it does not mean.)
  • What is the missing piece of information you need before you can take this finding seriously?
  • If the study power was 0.5, what does that tell you about the reliability of this estimate?
  • If the same researchers also ran 19 other tests on the same data and only this one came out significant, how should that change your interpretation?

storyBeats.text: Master Vesper sets a single sheet of parchment in front of you. On it: p = 0.04. Below the number she has written, in red, three question marks.

storyBeats.speaker: Master Vesper
storyBeats.text: Tell me what this number means. (she watches your face) No, more carefully. People will say it is the probability that the result was due to chance. They are wrong. They will say it is the probability the null is true. Wrong. They will say it is the probability the effect is real. Catastrophically wrong.

storyBeats.speaker: Master Vesper
storyBeats.text: It is the probability of seeing data at least this extreme if the null hypothesis were true. That is all. Read it back to yourself a hundred times if you must. The conditional matters. If the null. If. The p-value tells you nothing about whether the null is actually true — only how surprising the data would be if it were.

storyBeats.speaker: Same p, different stories
storyBeats.text:
Study A: n = 30,    d = 0.95,  p = 0.04
  Large effect, small sample, marginally significant.
  May be real but the estimate is noisy and inflated.

Study B: n = 30,000, d = 0.02,  p = 0.04
  Tiny effect, huge sample, marginally significant.
  Real but trivially small — clinically meaningless.

Study C: n = 30,    d = 0.95,  p = 0.04,
  but 19 other tests on the same data
  None reported.
  Garden of forking paths — likely false positive.

storyBeats.speaker: Master Vesper
storyBeats.text: Three studies. Three identical p-values. Three completely different things going on. A p-value without an effect size, a sample size, and the count of tests run is a number stripped of everything that gives it meaning. Do not be impressed by p < 0.05 alone. Ever.

storyBeats.speaker: Master Vesper
storyBeats.text: And remember Ioannidis. (she taps the parchment) In 2005 he published an essay titled "Why Most Published Research Findings Are False." The argument was Bayesian: in fields where most hypotheses are false a priori, where samples are small, where the temptation to keep testing is large — the posterior probability that a published p < 0.05 reflects a real effect can fall below half. The replication crisis you'll meet in the next lesson is the empirical confirmation. He was right.

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Your friend reads a headline: "New diet helps you lose weight (p = 0.03)." Explain in plain language what that p-value does and does not say, and what three pieces of additional information they need before deciding whether to believe the result.

questions.questionHtml: What does a p-value of 0.04 actually mean?
options: Assuming the null hypothesis is true, there is a 4% probability of observing data at least this extreme
There is a 4% probability that the null hypothesis is true
There is a 96% probability that the alternative hypothesis is true
The result has a 4% chance of being due to chance
questions.correctAnswer: Assuming the null hypothesis is true, there is a 4% probability of observing data at least this extreme
questions.explanationHtml: The p-value is conditional on H0 being true. It is P(data this extreme | H0). It says nothing about the probability that H0 itself is true — that's a Bayesian quantity that frequentist tests don't directly produce. Confusing the two is among the most common errors in scientific reasoning.

questions.questionHtml: Two studies report p = 0.04. Study A: n = 30, Cohen's d = 0.9. Study B: n = 30,000, Cohen's d = 0.02. Both are statistically significant. Which interpretation is correct?
options: Study A reports a large effect on a small sample (noisy but potentially meaningful); Study B reports a trivially small effect detected only because the huge sample gave high power. Statistical significance alone tells you nothing about practical significance.
Both are equally informative because they have the same p-value
Study B is more reliable because it has a bigger sample
Study A is more reliable because it found a bigger effect
questions.correctAnswer: Study A reports a large effect on a small sample (noisy but potentially meaningful); Study B reports a trivially small effect detected only because the huge sample gave high power. Statistical significance alone tells you nothing about practical significance.
questions.explanationHtml: p depends on both effect size and sample size. A huge sample can render a meaningless effect "significant"; a small sample with a real effect may miss significance. Effect size answers "how big is it?" — p answers only "how surprising is it under H0?". Both must be reported (APA standard since 1994/2010) for a result to be interpretable.

questions.questionHtml: A researcher analyses 20 different outcomes on the same dataset, each tested at α = 0.05. They report only the one significant result. What's the problem?
options: Even if no real effects exist, you'd expect about one false positive in 20 tests at α = 0.05 — the multiple-comparisons problem. Reporting only the significant one massively inflates the apparent strength of the finding.
There is no problem — significance is significance
The researcher should have used Cohen's d instead of p
Twenty outcomes is too few — should have done 100
questions.correctAnswer: Even if no real effects exist, you'd expect about one false positive in 20 tests at α = 0.05 — the multiple-comparisons problem. Reporting only the significant one massively inflates the apparent strength of the finding.
questions.explanationHtml: This is the multiple-comparisons problem (and its honest-researcher cousin, the garden of forking paths from Gelman & Loken 2014). With 20 tests, the family-wise probability of at least one false positive is ~64% under no real effects. Bonferroni or false-discovery-rate corrections, plus pre-registration of the analysis plan, are the standard defences.

questions.questionHtml: Statistical power is 0.80 in a study. Which statement is correct?
options: If a real effect of the assumed size exists, the study has an 80% chance of detecting it (rejecting the null) — and conversely a 20% chance of missing it (Type II error)
The study has an 80% chance of being correct overall
There is an 80% chance the result will be statistically significant regardless of whether the effect is real
Power has no relation to Type I or Type II errors
questions.correctAnswer: If a real effect of the assumed size exists, the study has an 80% chance of detecting it (rejecting the null) — and conversely a 20% chance of missing it (Type II error)
questions.explanationHtml: Power = 1 − β, where β is the Type II error rate. A power of 0.80 (the conventional target) means an 80% probability of correctly rejecting a false null — given the assumed effect size and sample size. Underpowered studies are not just more likely to miss real effects; when they DO hit significance, they systematically overstate effect size (Gelman & Carlin 2014).

subChunks.title: Peer Review & Replication
subChunks.hookHtml: A finding that has not been replicated is a rumour with a confidence interval. The system that turns rumours into knowledge is peer review and replication — and as you will see, the system has been quietly failing for decades.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
How peer review works

When a researcher submits a paper to a journal, the editor sends it to two or three subject-matter experts (peer reviewers) who read it and recommend accept, revise, or reject. The reviewers do this unpaid and largely anonymously. Three common variants exist:

  • Single-blind — reviewers know the authors; authors don't know the reviewers. Most common in many fields. Vulnerable to authority bias.
  • Double-blind — neither side knows the other. Reduces bias but is harder to implement when authors are identifiable from preprints, citations, or method.
  • Open — both sides are known, often with reviews published alongside the paper. Increases accountability.

What peer review catches — and what it does not

Peer review is good at catching: methodological errors a domain expert would notice, missing controls, statistical mistakes, citations to the wrong literature, claims that overreach the data. It is not good at catching: outright fabrication, p-hacking that fits the surface form of legitimate analysis, plausible-sounding analyses that depend on undocumented researcher choices, or replication failures that only surface when someone re-runs the experiment. Reviewers cannot inspect the raw data unless asked, cannot rerun the analysis without considerable effort, and rarely have time to do so.

The replication crisis

In 2015, the Open Science Collaboration published "Estimating the reproducibility of psychological science" in Science. They had attempted to replicate 100 published psychological findings using protocols pre-approved by the original authors. The headline result: only ~36% of the original findings replicated at conventional statistical thresholds, and the average effect size in replications was about half the original. Subsequent large-scale replication projects in cancer biology, economics, and clinical medicine found similar — sometimes worse — replication rates.

The crisis is not that scientists are dishonest. It is that the combined incentives of publish-or-perish, the multiple-comparisons problem, the garden of forking paths (sci-a3), and a publication bias toward positive results produce a body of literature in which a meaningful fraction of "established" findings are not real. Ioannidis (2005) had warned of exactly this; the OSC2015 paper showed it.

What goes wrong (and gives science a way back)

Two practices in particular were normalised before being recognised as corrupting:

  • HARKing — "Hypothesizing After Results are Known." The researcher runs the data, finds whatever pattern is significant, and writes the introduction as if that had been the prediction all along. The reader cannot distinguish a confirmed prediction from a post-hoc story; the false-positive rate inflates.
  • p-hacking — trying multiple analyses until one reaches p < 0.05, and reporting only that one. Includes: dropping outliers, adding covariates, transforming variables, peeking at data and stopping when significant, splitting the sample. Each individually defensible; in combination, deadly.

Pre-registration and registered reports

The corrective is to commit, in writing and on a public registry, to the hypothesis, design, sample size, and analysis plan before seeing the data. Pre-registration (e.g. on the Open Science Framework, AsPredicted) makes deviations from the plan auditable. Registered Reports go further: peer review happens on the methodology before data collection, and acceptance is conditional on doing what was promised — not on whether the result "worked." Registered Reports break the link between novelty/positivity and publishability that drove the crisis. They are slowly spreading; they are not yet the default.

The replication crisis is not a death-blow to science. It is the immune response. The fields that took it seriously — psychology in particular — are demonstrably better at producing durable findings now than they were in 2010. The lesson for a careful reader: a single significant paper is a hypothesis, not a fact. A finding becomes fact when independent labs, ideally with pre-registered protocols, get the same answer.
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
📜 Audit a paper

Pick any psychology or biomedical paper that's at least five years old. (PubMed and PsycNet are good sources.) Then check:

  • Was a hypothesis pre-registered? (Look for an OSF / AsPredicted link in the methods.)
  • Has it been replicated? (Try Google Scholar's "Cited by" list and search for "replication" or "failed to replicate.")
  • What was the sample size, and would a power calculation for the reported effect size have suggested it was adequate?
  • Were the analyses simple and few, or was every reported test one of many possible decisions?

Most papers from before 2015 will not survive this audit cleanly. That is the point of the exercise.

storyBeats.text: Master Vesper opens a heavy ledger marked Findings Withdrawn. The pages are dense with names, titles, dates.

storyBeats.speaker: Master Vesper
storyBeats.text: Every entry in this ledger is a paper that did not survive someone trying to repeat it. Some were honest mistakes — small samples, unlucky data, results that should have been read as suggestive but were written as definitive. A few were deliberate. The vast majority were neither — they were the predictable output of a system that rewarded novelty over reliability.

storyBeats.speaker: Master Vesper
storyBeats.text: In 2015, a group called the Open Science Collaboration tried to replicate one hundred well-known psychology findings, using protocols the original authors had signed off on. About thirty-six replicated at conventional thresholds. Average effect sizes shrank by half. Cancer biology has been worse. Economics has been comparable. This was not a fringe finding. It was the field measuring its own foundations and finding cracks.

storyBeats.speaker: Two practices that broke the system
storyBeats.text:
HARKing
  ("Hypothesizing After Results are Known")
  Run the data, find the pattern,
  rewrite the introduction so the
  pattern appears predicted.
  Reader cannot tell what was prediction
  vs post-hoc story.

p-hacking
  Try many analyses; report only those
  that crossed p < 0.05.
  Each individually defensible.
  In combination, the false-positive rate
  detonates.

storyBeats.speaker: Master Vesper
storyBeats.text: The corrective is simple and uncomfortable: commit, in writing, on a public registry, to your hypothesis, your sample size, and your analysis plan before you collect the data. We call this pre-registration. The fiercer version is the registered report — peer review of the methodology happens before data collection, and the journal commits to publish based on the design, not the outcome. This breaks the link between novelty and publishability that drove the crisis.

storyBeats.speaker: Master Vesper
storyBeats.text: And here is the thing to take home, apprentice. (she closes the ledger) Peer review is necessary but not sufficient. A single peer-reviewed paper is a hypothesis with editorial confidence — it is not yet a fact. A finding becomes fact when independent labs, ideally with pre-registered protocols, get the same answer. Until then, hold it gently.

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend who has just read a single "groundbreaking" study why a careful reader does not yet treat it as established knowledge. Mention HARKing, p-hacking, and the OSC 2015 replication results without using jargon.

questions.questionHtml: What did the Open Science Collaboration's 2015 replication project find?
options: Roughly 36% of 100 attempted replications of psychology studies reproduced the original findings at conventional statistical thresholds, with average effect sizes about half the original
All published psychology findings replicated successfully
About 90% of psychology findings replicated, confirming the field's reliability
Replication is impossible because every experiment is unique
questions.correctAnswer: Roughly 36% of 100 attempted replications of psychology studies reproduced the original findings at conventional statistical thresholds, with average effect sizes about half the original
questions.explanationHtml: The Open Science Collaboration's 2015 paper in Science attempted 100 replications using author-approved protocols. About 36% reached statistical significance in the same direction; average effect sizes shrank by roughly half. Similar projects in cancer biology, economics, and clinical medicine found comparable rates.

questions.questionHtml: What is HARKing?
options: Hypothesizing After Results are Known — running the data, finding what's significant, then writing the introduction as if that had been the prediction
A statistical correction for multiple comparisons
A specific software package used in psychology research
Anonymous reviewing of journal submissions
questions.correctAnswer: Hypothesizing After Results are Known — running the data, finding what's significant, then writing the introduction as if that had been the prediction
questions.explanationHtml: HARKing converts a post-hoc observation into a fake confirmed prediction. The reader cannot distinguish it from a genuine pre-registered hypothesis, so the false-positive rate of the literature inflates. Pre-registration is the standard fix — it makes the analysis plan auditable.

questions.questionHtml: Pre-registration and Registered Reports both aim to fix problems with the literature, but they differ. What's the key difference?
options: Pre-registration commits the analysis plan to a public registry before data collection. Registered Reports go further: peer review happens on the methodology BEFORE data are collected, and acceptance is conditional on doing what was promised — not on whether the result "worked"
There is no difference — they are the same procedure under different names
Pre-registration is for psychology; Registered Reports are for biology
Registered Reports are private; pre-registration is public
questions.correctAnswer: Pre-registration commits the analysis plan to a public registry before data collection. Registered Reports go further: peer review happens on the methodology BEFORE data are collected, and acceptance is conditional on doing what was promised — not on whether the result "worked"
questions.explanationHtml: Both aim to break the link between getting the "right" result and getting published. Pre-registration makes deviations auditable. Registered Reports go further by accepting papers based on methodology, regardless of outcome — this is the strongest defence against publication bias toward positive findings.

questions.questionHtml: A press release describes a single new psychology study with a striking finding. The study has not been pre-registered or replicated. What's the appropriate response of a scientifically literate reader?
options: Treat it as a hypothesis with editorial confidence — interesting but not yet established. Reserve belief until at least one independent, ideally pre-registered, replication produces the same effect
Accept it as fact because peer review is sufficient validation
Reject it entirely because all single studies are wrong
Believe it only if it confirms what you already thought
questions.correctAnswer: Treat it as a hypothesis with editorial confidence — interesting but not yet established. Reserve belief until at least one independent, ideally pre-registered, replication produces the same effect
questions.explanationHtml: Peer review is necessary but not sufficient. Reviewers can catch many errors but cannot easily detect p-hacking, HARKing, fabrication, or replication failures. The OSC 2015 results suggest a substantial fraction of single peer-reviewed findings will not replicate — and that fraction varies by field. Independent replication, ideally pre-registered, is what turns a finding into established knowledge.

subChunks.title: Pseudoscience Detection
subChunks.hookHtml: The hardest part of pseudoscience detection is that pseudoscience does not look like pseudoscience. It uses the language of evidence, the cadence of expertise, the apparatus of citation. The diagnostic is structural — what the claim does when challenged.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Falsifiability — and its limits

Popper's demarcation criterion (sci-a1) was: a claim is scientific if and only if it is, in principle, falsifiable. This was a useful sword for cutting through 20th-century pseudoscience. But it is too sharp at the edges. Imre Lakatos (1970) pointed out that real science does not give up on a theory the moment a single observation contradicts it — every theory swims in a sea of contradicting observations, and good scientists usually treat them as anomalies to be explained rather than refutations.

Lakatos refined Popper: science is not pure falsification but a research programme that makes progressive predictions — predictions that anticipate previously unknown phenomena, which then turn out to be true. A research programme is degenerating when it survives only by absorbing contradictions through ad-hoc modifications that explain nothing new. Falsifiability remains useful; degenerating research programmes are the more honest signal in practice.

Hallmarks of pseudoscience

No single hallmark is decisive — fringe science has often shared some — but the cluster is diagnostic.

HallmarkWhat it looks like
Unfalsifiable claimsThe claim is structured so no possible observation could contradict it
Ad hoc rescuesEach failed prediction triggers a small modification that preserves the theory but explains nothing new
Conspiracy framing"Mainstream science suppresses this" — sceptical findings are treated as evidence of cover-up rather than evidence against
No progressive predictionsThe theory has not, over decades, anticipated phenomena that were then independently confirmed
Appeals to authority / antiquity"Ancient wisdom," "used for thousands of years," or a single charismatic founder cited as proof
Confirmation by anecdoteHeavy reliance on testimonials; reluctance to engage with controlled trials
Vague, motte-and-bailey claimsA bold claim is asserted publicly; when challenged, it retreats to a trivially true version, then re-emerges later
Misuse of scientific vocabularyWords like "energy," "frequency," "quantum" used metaphorically but presented as physical mechanisms

Worked examples

  • Homeopathy — the central claim (substances become more potent the more they are diluted, eventually past the point of any molecule remaining) is in direct contradiction with chemistry and pharmacology. Numerous large RCTs and meta-analyses (e.g. Shang et al. 2005 in The Lancet) have found effects indistinguishable from placebo. The response within homeopathy has been ad-hoc rescues ("water memory") rather than abandonment.
  • Astrology — birth charts and personality predictions are routinely found unable to distinguish individuals at better than chance in blinded tests (e.g. Carlson 1985 in Nature). The response has been to retreat from specific predictions toward vague descriptive language that any reader could ratify (the Forer effect).
  • "Energy" healing — claims about manipulating life-force energies are unfalsifiable in their strongest form; in their weakest form (clinically detectable energy fields) they have been tested. Rosa et al. (1998 in JAMA) ran a blinded test in which therapeutic-touch practitioners could not detect the experimenter's hand at better than chance.
  • Anti-vaccine frameworks — the original (Wakefield 1998, retracted 2010) was research fraud. The response from the framework has been not to abandon the conclusion but to shift the proposed mechanism (mercury → aluminium → "too many too soon" → spike protein), the conspiracy framing escalating with each disconfirmation. This is degeneration in Lakatos's sense.

When fringe claims turn out to be science

Be careful: "fringe" is not the same as "pseudoscience." Continental drift was treated as nonsense for decades — Wegener (1912) was ridiculed; the theory was vindicated only in the 1960s when plate-tectonic evidence accumulated. Helicobacter pylori as the cause of most peptic ulcers was widely dismissed before Marshall & Warren (1984) provided controlled evidence (and a self-experiment). Prions were considered absurd before being established by Prusiner (Nobel Prize 1997).

The difference between a vindicated fringe claim and pseudoscience is not whether the establishment initially dismissed it — both are dismissed. The difference is what the proponents did: continental drift accumulated progressive predictions about magnetic seafloor stripes, fossil distributions, and earthquake belts, all of which were then independently confirmed. Homeopathy, two centuries on, has not produced one such prediction. The asymmetry is everything.

How to read a Methods section

This is the practical close-out of sci-a. When you read the Methods section of a paper, ask:

  1. Was the hypothesis pre-registered?
  2. Are the IV, DV, and operational definitions explicitly stated?
  3. Is there a control group? Was assignment random? Was the study blinded?
  4. Is the sample size justified by a power calculation?
  5. Are the analyses simple and few? Is each reported test the only one run, or one of many?
  6. Are effect sizes and confidence intervals reported alongside p-values?
  7. Has the finding been independently replicated?

If most of those answers are yes, the paper deserves serious attention. If most are no, you have a hypothesis with editorial confidence — interesting, but not yet knowledge.
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
📜 Diagnose a claim

Pick a claim circulating in popular media that you suspect is pseudoscientific. (Recent examples: "detox" diets, crystal healing, biorhythms, specific astrology predictions.) For your chosen claim:

  • State the claim precisely. What predictions does it make?
  • Is the claim, as stated, falsifiable in principle? If yes, what observation would refute it?
  • Has the claim been put to a controlled, blinded test? What happened?
  • How does the claim's community respond to disconfirming evidence — by revising the claim, or by ad-hoc rescues / conspiracy framing?
  • Has the claim, in 50+ years of existence, made any progressive predictions that were later independently confirmed?

Now do the same exercise with continental drift as it would have looked in 1925, when it was "fringe." Notice the difference.

storyBeats.text: Master Vesper sets two flasks side by side. One bears a label in elegant script: Tonic of Vital Essence — used since the third dynasty. The other is unlabeled.

storyBeats.speaker: Master Vesper
storyBeats.text: Pseudoscience does not announce itself. It uses our vocabulary. It cites studies. It speaks of energy and balance and frequency. The diagnostic is not in the language but in the structure — what the claim does when you challenge it.

storyBeats.speaker: Master Vesper
storyBeats.text: Popper said: a claim is scientific if it is falsifiable. Useful sword. Lakatos refined it: real science does not abandon a theory at the first contradiction — every good theory swims in anomalies. The honest signal is whether the research programme is progressive: does it make new predictions that come true? Or does it survive only by absorbing each failure with a small ad-hoc patch that explains nothing new?

storyBeats.speaker: The pseudoscience diagnostic cluster
storyBeats.text:
Watch for the pattern:

  - Claims structured so nothing could refute them
  - Failed predictions triggering ad-hoc rescues
    rather than abandonment
  - Conspiracy framing of skeptics
  - No progressive predictions in 50+ years
  - Appeals to ancient wisdom or charismatic
    founders as proof
  - Heavy reliance on testimonials, resistance
    to controlled trials
  - Motte-and-bailey: bold claim retreats to
    trivial claim under pressure, re-emerges
    later unchanged
  - Words like 'energy', 'quantum', 'frequency'
    used metaphorically but presented as physics

storyBeats.speaker: Master Vesper
storyBeats.text: Be careful, though. Fringe is not pseudoscience. Continental drift was ridiculed for fifty years before plate tectonics vindicated it. Helicobacter pylori as the cause of ulcers was rejected before Marshall and Warren provided controlled evidence. Prions were absurd before they were a Nobel Prize. The establishment dismisses both — vindicated science and pseudoscience. The difference is what happens next.

storyBeats.speaker: Master Vesper
storyBeats.text: Continental drift made progressive predictions: magnetic stripes on the seafloor would alternate; fossil distributions would map onto reconstructed coastlines; earthquakes would cluster on plate boundaries. All confirmed. Homeopathy, two centuries on, has produced no such prediction. That asymmetry is everything. Now go — read a Methods section. You have everything you need to find the cracks.

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend the difference between continental drift in 1925 (fringe but on the path to becoming science) and homeopathy today (pseudoscience). Show how the structural hallmarks — progressive predictions vs ad-hoc rescues — distinguish the two even when both are rejected by the mainstream of their day.

questions.questionHtml: Continental drift was dismissed by mainstream geology for decades before being vindicated. Homeopathy is also dismissed by mainstream medicine. What is the structural difference between a vindicated fringe claim and pseudoscience?
options: Vindicated fringe theories accumulate progressive predictions — new phenomena they anticipate, which are later independently confirmed. Pseudoscience makes no such predictions and survives by ad-hoc rescues
There is no difference; mainstream rejection is the only criterion that matters
Vindicated fringe theories are always rejected at first because they are too revolutionary
Pseudoscience is rejected because it is too mathematical for the mainstream
questions.correctAnswer: Vindicated fringe theories accumulate progressive predictions — new phenomena they anticipate, which are later independently confirmed. Pseudoscience makes no such predictions and survives by ad-hoc rescues
questions.explanationHtml: Lakatos's progressive-vs-degenerating research programme is the cleanest distinction. Continental drift predicted magnetic seafloor stripes, fossil distributions, and earthquake belts — all later confirmed. Homeopathy in two centuries has produced no such confirmed novel prediction. Mainstream rejection alone is not the criterion; what matters is whether the programme generates predictions that the world ratifies.

questions.questionHtml: What is an "ad hoc rescue" in the context of evaluating a theory?
options: A modification made to a theory specifically to avoid a falsifying observation, but that explains nothing new and predicts nothing further
A new experiment designed to confirm an established finding
A peer review correction to a published paper
A statistical adjustment for multiple comparisons
questions.correctAnswer: A modification made to a theory specifically to avoid a falsifying observation, but that explains nothing new and predicts nothing further
questions.explanationHtml: Ad-hoc rescues are how degenerating research programmes (Lakatos 1970) survive contradicting evidence. The theory is patched just enough to fit the failed prediction, but the patch makes no further predictions of its own. Repeated ad-hoc rescues are a hallmark of pseudoscience. Compare with science, where contradicting evidence either revises the theory in a way that generates new predictions or eventually leads to abandoning it.

questions.questionHtml: Two claims are being defended publicly. Which is more likely to be pseudoscience, based purely on structural features?
options: Claim B: When pressed for evidence, defenders cite ancient lineage, dismiss skeptics as agents of suppression, and respond to each failed clinical trial with a new modification of the proposed mechanism
Claim A: Defenders point to peer-reviewed RCTs, acknowledge null replications, and explain the proposed mechanism in terms compatible with established physics
There is no way to tell without doing the experiments yourself
Whichever claim is older is more likely to be true
questions.correctAnswer: Claim B: When pressed for evidence, defenders cite ancient lineage, dismiss skeptics as agents of suppression, and respond to each failed clinical trial with a new modification of the proposed mechanism
questions.explanationHtml: This is the classic pseudoscience cluster: appeal to antiquity, conspiracy framing of skeptics, and ad-hoc mechanism shifts after each failed test. Claim A's behaviour — engaging with peer-reviewed evidence, acknowledging null findings, sticking to mechanisms compatible with established physics — is the structural pattern of legitimate science even when it turns out to be wrong.

questions.questionHtml: You read a Methods section that has: (a) no pre-registration, (b) no control group, (c) no power calculation, (d) reports only p-values without effect sizes, and (e) presents conclusions as established. How should a careful reader respond?
options: Treat the conclusions as untested speculation. The design lacks the safeguards that turn data into evidence — without controls and pre-registration, there is no way to distinguish a real effect from confounds, expectancy, or post-hoc analysis. The paper is a hypothesis at best
Accept the conclusions because the paper passed peer review
Reject the paper entirely as fraud
Believe the conclusions only if they confirm prior beliefs
questions.correctAnswer: Treat the conclusions as untested speculation. The design lacks the safeguards that turn data into evidence — without controls and pre-registration, there is no way to distinguish a real effect from confounds, expectancy, or post-hoc analysis. The paper is a hypothesis at best
questions.explanationHtml: A paper missing those five elements has not earned the right to assert conclusions. Pre-registration audits the analysis plan; controls rule out confounds; power calculations justify whether the sample could detect the claimed effect; effect sizes show whether the result matters in practice; replication is what turns it into knowledge. A peer-reviewed paper missing all five is the literature equivalent of a hypothesis: interesting, but not yet established.
